entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen19346" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19347" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19348" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19348" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19347" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19349" type="x-p"/> The psalmist appeals to God for his integrity, and desires to be brought to the Divine test in order to have his innocence proved, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.1-Psa.26.3">Psa 26:1-3</reference>; shows that he had avoided all fellowship with the wicked, and associated unth the upright, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.4-Psa.26.8">Psa 26:4-8</reference>; prays that he may not have his final lot with the workers of iniquity, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.9">Psa 26:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.10">Psa 26:10</reference>; purposes to walk uprightly before God, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.11">Psa 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.26.12">Psa 26:12</reference>. <div eID="gen19349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19350" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, and the two following, are supposed by Calmet to be all parts of one ode, and to relate to the time of the captivity, containing the prayers, supplications, complaints, and resolutions of the Israelites in Babylon. This is probable; but we have not evidence enough to authorize us to be nice on such points. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen19350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19352" type="x-p"/> Judge me, O Lord - There are so many strong assertions in this Psalm concerning the innocence and uprightness of its author that many suppose he wrote it to vindicate himself from some severe reflections on his conduct or accusations relative to plots, conspiracies, etc. This seems to render the opinion probable that attributes it to David during his exile, when all manner of false accusations were brought against him at the court of Saul. <div eID="gen19352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19353" type="x-p"/> I have walked in mine integrity - I have never plotted against the life nor property of any man; I have neither coveted nor endeavored to possess myself of Saul's crown. <div eID="gen19353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19354" type="x-p"/> I have trusted - Had I acted otherwise, I could not have been prosperous, for thou wouldst not have worked miracles for the preservation of a wicked man. <div eID="gen19354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19355" type="x-p"/> I shall not slide - I shall be preserved from swerving from the paths of righteousness and truth.
entries.content_plain: Introduction The psalmist appeals to God for his integrity, and desires to be brought to the Divine test in order to have his innocence proved, Psa 26:1-3 ; shows that he had avoided all fellowship with the wicked, and associated unth the upright, Psa 26:4-8 ; prays that he may not have his final lot with the workers of iniquity, Psa 26:9 , Psa 26:10 ; purposes to walk uprightly before God, Psa 26:11 , Psa 26:12 . This Psalm, and the two following, are supposed by Calmet to be all parts of one ode, and to relate to the time of the captivity, containing the prayers, supplications, complaints, and resolutions of the Israelites in Babylon. This is probable; but we have not evidence enough to authorize us to be nice on such points. See on Psa 26:1 (note). Verse 1 Judge me, O Lord - There are so many strong assertions in this Psalm concerning the innocence and uprightness of its author that many suppose he wrote it to vindicate himself from some severe reflections on his conduct or accusations relative to plots, conspiracies, etc. This seems to render the opinion probable that attributes it to David during his exile, when all manner of false accusations were brought against him at the court of Saul. I have walked in mine integrity - I have never plotted against the life nor property of any man; I have neither coveted nor endeavored to possess myself of Saul's crown. I have trusted - Had I acted otherwise, I could not have been prosperous, for thou wouldst not have worked miracles for the preservation of a wicked man. I shall not slide - I shall be preserved from swerving from the paths of righteousness and truth.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19360" type="x-p"/> I have hated the congregation of evil doers - I have never made one in the crowds of discontented persons; persons who, under pretense of rectifying what was wrong in the state, strove to subvert it, to breed general confusion, to overturn the laws, seize on private property, and enrich themselves by the spoils of the country.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19361" type="x-p"/> I will wash mine hands in innocency - Washing the hands was frequent among the Jews, and was sometimes an action by which a man declared his innocence of any base or wicked transaction. This Pilate did, to protest his innocence of the mal-treatment and death of Christ. I will maintain that innocence of life in which I have hitherto walked; and take care that nothing shall be found in my heart or life that would prevent me from using the most holy ordinance, or worshipping thee in spirit and truth. <div eID="gen19361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19362" type="x-p"/> So wilt I compass thine altar - It is a mark of respect among the Hindoos to walk several times round a superior, and round a temple.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19364" type="x-p"/> Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house - I have carefully used thine ordinances, that I might obtain more grace to help me to persevere. And I have not been attentive to those duties, merely because they were incumbent on me; but I have loved the place where thine honor dwelleth; and my delight in thy ordinances has made my attendance as pleasant as it was profitable. This verse would be better translated, Jehovah, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place of the tabernacle of thy glory. The habitation must mean the holy of holies, where the Divine Presence was manifest; and the place of the tabernacle must refer to the mercy-seat, or the place where the glory of the Lord appeared between the cherubim, upon the lid or cover of the ark of the covenant. From his dwelling there, משכן mishcan, the place and the appearance were called שכינה shechinah; the dwelling of Jehovah, or that glorious appearance which was the symbol of the Divine Presence.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19370" type="x-p"/> My foot standeth in an even place - On the above principles I have taken my stand: to abhor evil; to cleave to that which is good; to avoid the company of wicked men; to frequent the ordinances of God; to be true and just in all my dealings with men; and to depend for my support and final salvation on the mere mercy of God. He who acts in this way, his feet stand in an even place. <div eID="gen19370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19371" type="x-p"/> I will bless the Lord - In all my transactions with men, and in all my assemblings with holy people, I will speak good of the name of the Lord, having nothing but good to speak of that name.  <chapter eID="Ps.26"/> <div eID="gen19371" type="x-p"/>
